summary:
Cabo Verde does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 71 of the 1886 Penal Code had prohibited unnatural acts; a 2004 amendment removed all provisions on consensual homosexual sex, making Cabo Verde the second African country to decriminalise after South Africa. The age of consent stood at 16 at decriminalisation, the same as for heterosexual acts, and was 14 as of 2015.

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. Civil law blocked the change to a female legal name sought by Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed transgender woman in Cabo Verde, who came out in 1997 at age 19 and in a local newspaper in 1998. The sources contain no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility. Transgender people in the country are often referred to locally as tchindas.

Articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code have banned workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation since 2008, with a fine set case by case. Article 406(3) extends the same penalty to unlawful dismissal on grounds of race, ethnic group, religion, sexual orientation or any other discriminatory reason. Gender identity is not covered by the protection as the sources describe it.

Cabo Verde does not recognise same-sex unions, and a trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local law has no recognition route. On 11 July 2017 Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva said legalisation of same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from the opposition of MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro. During 2018 Pride Week in Praia, NGOs petitioned the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law.

Andrade describes Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reports verbal violence and two physical attacks. No trans-specific violence statistics are on record.

A 2020 Afrobarometer poll found 80% of Cape Verdeans would welcome or would not be bothered by having a homosexual neighbour, one of only four African countries polled with a majority in favour; 2019 to 2021 polling put acceptance of a homosexual neighbour at 82%. Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 of May 2020 names Cabo Verde among particularly tolerant countries while noting that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains weak even among younger respondents. Every tolerance finding in the sources is framed around gays, lesbians, homosexual neighbours or LGBT people generally; no equivalent data on attitudes toward transgender people is on record.

The 2010 U.S. Department of State human rights report cited in the sources found that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity continued to be a problem, and that no LGBT organisations were active in the country at that time.

LGBTIQ organisations register freely. Associação Gay de Cabo Verde was established by 2013, the first pride parade was held in Mindelo in June 2013 as the second such event in Africa, and the first Praia pride followed three years later. The 2018 Praia Pride was organised with the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and the Praia municipal government.

Cabo Verde signed the 18 December 2008 UN General Assembly statement, joined by 65 other states, affirming that human rights apply regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity, and backed a 2011 statement condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people. It is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group and made anti-discrimination commitments at the 2024 Universal Periodic Review. On 28 June 2025 it was the only African country to join a 15-state joint declaration that rejects violence, criminalisation, stigmatisation and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, supports eradicating transphobic harassment and promoting socio-labour inclusion especially for trans persons, calls for the repeal of and refusal to introduce laws punishing sexual orientation and gender identity, demands an end to criminal prosecution including imprisonment and the death penalty and to conversion practices, and commits public authorities to implement LGBTIQ+ equality under international human rights standards.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 declaration commitments on conversion practices, transphobic harassment and socio-labour inclusion for trans persons have no counterpart in the domestic record, which holds no statute on gender identity, no gender recognition procedure and no ban on conversion practices.

Regional comparison runs in Cabo Verde's favour on several measures: decriminalisation in 2004 made it the second African country to do so, the 2013 Mindelo parade was the second pride event in Africa, and the 2025 declaration was signed as the only African country among 15.

The 2010 State Department finding that no LGBT organisations were active contrasts with organisations registered by 2013 and with pride events held from 2013 onward.

Tolerance polling measures attitudes toward gay and lesbian neighbours. It does not measure attitudes toward transgender people, so it cannot be read as a trans-specific safety indicator.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources contain no statute, provision, penalty or procedure on legal gender recognition, change of gender markers on documents, screening, segregated facilities, custody or medical care for transgender people.

No trans-specific violence statistics and no hate-crime protection data are on record. The only trans-specific violence account is one individual's report of verbal abuse and two physical attacks.

No documented statement about societal tolerance specifically toward transgender people appears in the sources; all tolerance findings are framed around gays, lesbians, homosexual neighbours or LGBT people generally.
